A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VLSBench and the same visual safety information leakage problem. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material across renaming and relocation.

before.justification: v2 reports original leakage measurements, textual versus multimodal alignment experiments, VLSBench model evaluations and category-level results.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds DPO comparisons, additional model evaluations, human evaluator checks, prompting experiments and input-modality analyses.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix H introduce a safety prompt that directs image-context analysis before answering, and an inference variant replacing images with generated captions. The central four-stage benchmark construction pipeline and its generation, detoxification and filtering procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds question-only, caption-based and image-only NSFW evaluation scenarios using existing VLSBench data. The underlying datasets and safety categories remain unchanged. Both appendices report 2,241 VLSBench pairs; the main-text change from 2.4k to 2.2k is a correction. FigStep is relabeled SafeBench with matching source, task and retained results.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds textual DPO, multimodal DPO for additional base models, and Chakraborty-style textual unlearning. v2's unlearning implementation is retained as SafeUnlearning, rather than replaced. VLSBench comparisons expand to InternVL2.5, MiniCPM, GLM, reasoning models and Claude3.5; the new prompting experiment also evaluates the MMSafetyBench prompt.

E3.justification: New protocols include multimodal/textual DPO using the same 30k preference examples with images removed for textual training, a proportionally selected 500-example prompting subset, and a 200-example caption-input subset. Appendix G adds balanced and per-label human validation designs, while Appendix C adds GPT-4o leakage verification. Existing SFT hyperparameter settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands analyses of evaluator validity, dependence on image input, safety-prompt effectiveness, NSFW detectability, model scale and reasoning capability. These include GPT-4o cross-verification in Appendix C and quantitative human checks in Tables 13–15. The earlier category radar plots and three detailed case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added human-validation accuracies and sample counts describe evaluation designs and point estimates, without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Numerous results are added, including Claude3.5-sonnet's 94.74% VLSBench safety rate, exceeding the earlier best closed-source result of 49.78% for Gemini-1.5-pro. Table 2 changes vanilla Qwen2-VL's MMVet score from 30.64 to 53.76. The LLaVA-7B textual-SFT MMSafetyBench average changes from 62.45 to 66.45 despite unchanged components averaging 62.45, so this is an inconsistent reported value, not an established gain.

T1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds mathematical definitions for the newly evaluated Chakraborty-style unlearning objective, including harmful/helpful losses, a KL utility term and their weighted combination. The VSIL definition, indicator-rate equations and SafeUnlearning objective are retained. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims about leakage, VLSBench and the relative suitability of textual versus multimodal alignment remain. v3 explicitly extends the claimed challenge across model sizes from 2B to 78B and adds alignment strategies as a contribution. Its abstract and conclusion also make the claimed reliability of cross-modal evaluation more explicit.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of human agreement, caption-based safety, low NSFW detection rates and Claude's exceptional performance, tentatively attributing the latter to safety preprocessing. Some interpretations exceed the evidence: the general claim that captions improve MLLM safety overlooks InternVL2.5's decline from 17.0% to 11.5% in Table 5. The original three limitations remain, relocated to the main text.

D1.justification: v3 adds unlearning weights, DPO image-handling details, judge and safety prompts, caption-generation information and detector identifiers. Existing SFT settings, hardware and construction prompts largely remain. The explicit statement about LLM-only fine-tuning with an all-black image disappears, without establishing a procedural change. The abstract replaces the project-site access pointer with a GitHub repository.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused from broad MLLM architecture and attack coverage toward safety alignment and benchmarks. Additions include MIS, ETA, RapGuard and MSSBench, while Appendix D and Table 8 develop explicit comparisons with alternatives including SIUO and MSSBench. This changes research positioning beyond citation-format updates.

P1.justification: The introduction, leakage explanation and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves to Appendix A, limitations and ethics move into the main text, and the appendices are reorganized around dedicated comparison, validation and supplementary-experiment sections. Terminology and dataset-count wording are also corrected.

P2.justification: Table 2 is reorganized into model-specific blocks with new color coding, and the former combined VLSBench table is split across main-text and appendix tables. Figures 1 and 6 are revised; the old Figure 7 alignment chart is replaced by a prompting chart, with its results retained elsewhere. Numerous comparison and validation tables are added, while appendix radar plots, cases and construction-prompt figures are retained.

improvement.justification: The matched-data DPO experiments and quantitative human validation substantially strengthen the central evidence: v2's SFT comparison used different training sources, and its VLSBench evaluator justification relied largely on qualitative illustration. Appendices E.4 and G address these important control and measurement gaps. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including the inconsistent MMSafetyBench average, a prompt result misquoted relative to Figure 7, and caption claims broader than Table 5 supports.
